target_customer: Retail investors who want to follow and copy other investors' trades
problem: Individuals wanted a way to share trade ideas with reasoning and let friends invest alongside them. Instavest let investors post trades, followers copy them, and the poster earn about 5 percent of profits.
business_model: Take rate on profit sharing (20 percent of the poster's roughly 5 percent cut), later paid newsletters

founders.name: Zain Allarakhia
founders.background_notes: Named as a founder with Khatri by TechCrunch on 2015-03-20; not listed on the YC page.

competitors.name: eToro
competitors.what: Social trading and CopyTrading network, launched a social trading product for younger traders in early 2015

competitors.name: Covestor
competitors.what: Platform for copying skilled investors, grouped with eToro and wikifolio as social investing alternatives to managed funds

technical_complexity.rationale: Required brokerage integrations (about ten brokerages by 2016) and trade mirroring workflows, a regulatory and integration heavy build for a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: Value would grow with active traders and followers, but eToro, Covestor and others already ran the model and brokerage integrations were available to rivals.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source found on incumbents copying or buying it. PitchBook lists it as out of business in February 2019.

market_need_then: In the closed beta reported by TechCrunch on 2015-03-20, 75 users committed 1.1 million dollars with an average account of 15,000 dollars, indicating early interest from active traders.

branding.domain_note: Used instavest.com; a Product Hunt commenter asked whether goInstavest.com was a rebrand, unconfirmed

brand_strength.rationale: Covered by TechCrunch at launch and at the seed round, but no source on the brand itself. Name clearly signals instant investing, though similar names exist such as InstaVest LLC.

outcome_analysis: Instavest raised a small round from YC, then a 1.7 million dollar seed in August 2016, and added brokerage integrations and paid newsletters. PitchBook and CB Insights list it as out of business or dead and PitchBook dates this to February 2019, but no shutdown statement or post-mortem was found, so the cause is not public. It competed with established social trading platforms like eToro and Covestor.
notes: The directory listed no website, so no company site was fetched. The 2016 round is stated by TechCrunch, Fintech Global and VC News Daily. The 2015 $120K round and the total of about $1.82M over four rounds come from PitchBook and CB Insights summaries (single databases), so one or more rounds may be missing. The shutdown date of 2019-02 rests on PitchBook alone. Competitor sources: the eToro item is from a Finovate page and the Covestor item from a 2014 Forrester report listing, both seen through search snippets only. TechCrunch 2015-03-20 named Wealthfront and Seed only as general fintech context, not competitors.
